lessons.title: A tour of the filesystem hierarchy
lessons.goal:
Learn what each top-level directory is for, so you know where to look for configuration, logs, programs and temporary files.

Why it matters: on any Linux machine you can find things fast if you know the standard layout (the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard).

setup.note: These commands only read the system. Output differs between distributions and machines.

steps.title: One tree, starting at /
steps.text: Linux has a single directory tree. Everything starts at `/` (root). There are no drive letters. Other disks are attached somewhere inside this tree.

run.output:
afs
bin
boot
dev
etc
home
lib
lib64
media
mnt
opt
proc
root
run
sbin
srv
sys
tmp
usr
var

steps.title: /etc: configuration
steps.text: `/etc` holds system-wide configuration as plain text files. Look here first when a service behaves differently than you expect.

run.output:
fstab
hosts
passwd
ssh
sudoers
systemd

steps.title: /usr: programs and libraries
steps.text: `/usr` holds most installed software. Programs are in `/usr/bin` and `/usr/sbin`, libraries in `/usr/lib64`. It should be read-only during normal use.

run.output:
bin
games
include
lib
lib64
libexec
local
sbin
share
src
tmp

steps.title: The old directories are links into /usr
steps.text: On modern distributions `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/lib` and `/lib64` are symbolic links into `/usr`. This is called the "usr merge". Old scripts that say `#!/bin/sh` still work.

run.output:
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 Oct 26  2024 /bin -> usr/bin
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 7 Oct 26  2024 /lib -> usr/lib
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 9 Oct 26  2024 /lib64 -> usr/lib64
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 8 Oct 26  2024 /sbin -> usr/sbin

steps.title: /var: data that changes
steps.text: `/var` holds data that grows while the system runs: logs (`/var/log`), package caches, spool queues, databases.

steps.title: /tmp, /home and /boot
steps.text: `/tmp` is for temporary files that anyone can create. It has the **sticky bit** (the `t`), so users cannot delete each other's files. `/home` holds user files. `/boot` holds the kernel and boot loader files.

run.output:
drwxr-xr-x.  3 root root   17 Sep 22 15:31 /home
drwxrwxrwt. 29 root root 4096 Nov  8 10:36 /tmp

steps.under: The standard is written down in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and summarised in `man hier`. It is a convention, not enforced by the kernel. The kernel only knows mount points and paths.

quiz.q: Where do you look first for the configuration of a service?
Where are log files normally written?
quiz.explain: /var holds data that changes at run time, including /var/log.

quiz.q: Why can you not delete another user's file in /tmp even though everyone can write there?
quiz.explain: With the sticky bit, only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root may delete or rename an entry.

quiz.q: On a modern system, what is /bin?

check.scenario: A disk fills up under /var/log. Name the directory tree you would check and the one command to find the biggest items.
check.answer: Check `/var/log` first. `du -xh /var/log --max-depth=1 | sort -h | tail` lists the largest subdirectories (`-x` stays on one filesystem). Then look inside the biggest one.

lessons.title: Everything is a file: /dev, /proc and /sys
lessons.goal:
Learn that devices, kernel data and system settings are exposed as files, and that some of those files are generated on the fly by the kernel.

Why it matters: because they look like files, you can inspect and tune the kernel with `cat`, `echo` and shell scripts.

setup.note: These commands only read the system. Output differs between distributions and machines.

steps.title: Devices are files in /dev
steps.text: A **device file** is a name that connects to a driver. The first letter of `ls -l` shows the type: `c` is a character device, `b` is a block device.

run.output:
crw-rw-rw-. 1 root root 1, 3 Sep 22 15:30 /dev/null
crw-rw-rw-. 1 root root 1, 9 Sep 22 15:30 /dev/urandom
crw-rw-rw-. 1 root root 1, 5 Sep 22 15:30 /dev/zero

steps.title: Read from and write to them like files
steps.text: `/dev/null` discards everything written to it. `/dev/zero` gives endless zero bytes. `/dev/urandom` gives random bytes. Any tool that reads a file works with them.

steps.title: /proc shows processes and kernel state
steps.text: `/proc` is a **pseudo filesystem**. Each process has a directory `/proc/PID`. Files like `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/loadavg` show kernel data.

steps.title: /sys shows devices and drivers
steps.text: `/sys` (sysfs) exposes the kernel's device model. Reading a file reads a value from a driver. Writing to some files changes a setting.

steps.title: Underneath: the content is generated when you read
steps.text: These files are **not stored on disk**. The kernel creates the text each time you read. That is why `stat` reports size 0 while `wc` finds bytes.

run.cmd: for d in /proc /sys /dev; do findmnt -no FSTYPE $d; done

steps.under: Each pseudo filesystem registers file operations with the VFS. When you `read()` a file in /proc, the kernel calls a function (for example `meminfo_proc_show`) that formats the current values into the buffer. No disk is involved.

quiz.q: Which first character in `ls -l` marks a block device?

options: The file is empty on disk
The content is generated by the kernel when read
stat is broken for text files
quiz.explain: Step 5: the file has no stored data. `wc -c` reads it and finds bytes.

quiz.q: Which file shows the kernel's load averages?
What happens to data written to /dev/null?
quiz.explain: The driver accepts the data and throws it away.

check.scenario: You need to know a process's command line and it has no `ps`-readable name. Which file do you read and why is it NUL-separated?
check.answer: `/proc/PID/cmdline`. It is the raw `argv` array copied from `execve`. Strings in C end with a NUL byte, so arguments are separated by NULs (`tr '\0' ' '` makes it readable).

lessons.title: Mount points, the usr merge and bind mounts
lessons.goal:
See how the single tree is built from several filesystems, and how to make the same directory appear in two places.

Why it matters: when `df` or a path behaves strangely, the cause is often a mount. Containers use the same mechanism.

setup.note: These commands only read the system. Output differs between distributions and machines.

steps.title: findmnt shows the tree of mounts
steps.text: Each mount attaches one filesystem to a directory. `findmnt` prints them as a tree. Here are the mounts of the top-level kernel filesystems.

run.output:
TARGET           FSTYPE
/proc            proc
/sys             sysfs
└─/sys/fs/cgroup cgroup2
/dev             devtmpfs
└─/dev/shm       tmpfs
/run             tmpfs
├─/run/user/1000 tmpfs
└─/run/user/988  tmpfs

steps.title: Which filesystem holds a path?
steps.text: `df` and `stat -f` tell you which filesystem a path lives on. `-T` adds the type.

steps.title: Mounts can hide files
steps.text: Mounting on a directory **hides** what was there. This is a classic trap: files written before the mount seem to vanish.
steps.after: After `umount` the original file is back. It was never deleted, only covered.

steps.title: A bind mount shows a directory in a second place
steps.text: `mount --bind A B` makes the directory A visible at B. There is no copy: both paths lead to the same files.
steps.under: The kernel keeps a table of mounts per **mount namespace**. A path lookup walks the dentry tree and, at each mount point, jumps to the root of the mounted filesystem. A bind mount adds an entry that points at an existing directory instead of a new filesystem. Containers (module 37) give each container its own table.

steps.title: Where the kernel lists its mounts
steps.text: The list is a file, `/proc/self/mountinfo`. Each line has the mount ID, parent ID, device, root, mount point and options.

run.output:
25 149 0:24 / /proc rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime shared:15 - proc proc rw
26 149 0:25 / /sys rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime shared:3 - sysfs sysfs rw,seclabel

quiz.q: You mount a filesystem on /data, which already had files. What happens to those files?
options: They are hidden until you unmount
quiz.explain: A mount covers the directory contents. They reappear after umount.
Both paths show the same files.

quiz.q: Which file lists the mounts of the current process's mount namespace?
quiz.explain: /etc/fstab is only configuration. mountinfo is the live table.

check.scenario: `df` says /var is 100% full but `du -sh /var` shows only half. Name two mount-related reasons.
check.answer:
1. Files hidden **under a mount point**: data was written to /var/xyz before another filesystem was mounted on /var/xyz. `du` cannot see it, `df` counts it. Unmount (or bind-mount the parent elsewhere) to look.
2. Deleted files still held open by a process (see module 18).

interview.a: /etc: configuration. /var: variable data (logs, caches, spools). /usr: installed programs and libraries. /tmp: temporary files for everyone, with the sticky bit. See [the tour](#/lesson/2/fhs-tour).

interview.q: What does "everything is a file" mean in Linux?
interview.a: Files, directories, devices, pipes, sockets and kernel data are accessed through the same file calls (`open`, `read`, `write`, `close`) and file descriptors. A driver or the kernel provides the content. See [the lesson](#/lesson/2/everything-is-a-file).
It is a pseudo file. The kernel generates the text when you read it, so there is no stored size.
/bin, /sbin, /lib and /lib64 are symbolic links to /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/lib, /usr/lib64. It lets /usr hold all vendor files, so it can be shared or mounted read-only.

interview.q: Files vanished after you mounted a disk on a directory. How do you get them back?
interview.a: They are hidden under the mount, not deleted. Unmount the disk, or bind-mount the parent filesystem somewhere else to see them. See [mounts](#/lesson/2/mounts-and-bind).

glossary.def: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: the agreed purpose of the top-level directories.
A file in /dev that connects to a kernel driver. Character (c) or block (b).
The pseudo filesystem on /proc with process and kernel information generated on read.
The pseudo filesystem on /sys that exposes the kernel's devices and drivers.
A directory where another filesystem is attached to the tree.
A mount that makes an existing directory visible at a second path without copying.
A permission bit on a directory: only the owner of an entry (or root) may delete or rename it. Shown as t, as on /tmp.
